content:
The Patna High Court’s decision in Sangita Kumari v. Surendra Kumar Himansu, M.A. No. 307 of 2015, decided on 26 March 2025, is significant for matrimonial jurisprudence because it reiterates that an allegation of adultery must be established by reliable evidence and cannot rest merely on suspicion or an uncorroborated allegation of having seen the spouse in a “compromising position.” 
More importantly, the Court observed that the allegation of adultery had not been supported by cogent, relevant and reliable evidence. Consequently, the husband failed to establish adultery as well as the alleged cruelty and desertion required for a decree of divorce. 
What is the legal principle?

Under Section 13(1)(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, voluntary sexual intercourse with a person other than the spouse after marriage constitutes a ground for divorce. Thus, the legally relevant question is not simply whether the spouse was seen with another person, but whether the evidence establishes the essential ingredients of adultery.
Adultery in India is no longer a criminal offence following the Supreme Court’s decision in Joseph Shine v. Union of India. However, adultery continues to be a civil/matrimonial ground for divorce under the Hindu Marriage Act.

Therefore:
Criminal prosecution for adultery ≠ matrimonial proof of adultery.
Why this judgment matters
This ruling sends a balanced message:
“Suspicion may create doubt, but suspicion alone cannot become proof.”
At the same time, the judgment should not be interpreted as giving immunity to genuine adulterous conduct. Where credible and convincing evidence establishes an extramarital sexual relationship, adultery can still constitute a valid ground for divorce.
The Court also examined the allegation of cruelty. It emphasized that ordinary disagreements, occasional harsh words or trivial incidents of married life cannot automatically be elevated to the level of legally recognised matrimonial cruelty. Specific facts and reliable evidence are important. 

My considered view

The judgment reflects an important principle of fairness in matrimonial litigation. Divorce proceedings should not become a mechanism for making serious allegations without adequate proof. At the same time, courts must remain sensitive to the fact that adultery generally takes place in private and therefore may often have to be proved through circumstantial evidence rather than direct evidence.

Hence, the correct legal position is:

“Compromising position may be a circumstance, but it is not automatically conclusive proof of adultery. The court must assess the credibility, consistency and totality of the evidence.”

This approach protects both sides—it prevents an innocent spouse from being condemned merely on suspicion, while preserving the right of a genuinely aggrieved spouse to obtain matrimonial relief when adultery is properly established.
comment: A key practical issue is the evidentiary challenge in private relationships—courts often have to balance circumstantial proof with the risk of reputational harm from untested allegations.
